speakeroldname: Hon. Waller L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF INVESTMENT CORPORATION
speechtext:
that the House go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following resolution, which has been recommended to the House by His Excellency:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish an investment corporation, to be known as the Canada Development Corporation, to provide through savings by Canadians a supplementary large-scale source of financing where substantial sums of equity capital are required for the initiation or expansion of larger enterprises in Canada and for facilitating, in the case of offers to purchase or sell shares of such enterprises, the acquisition of such shares by Canadian residents rather than non-residents; to authorize the issue by the Corporation to Canadian residents, at an initial issue price of five dollars per share, of shares of the Corporation the total number of which outstanding at any time shall not exceed two hundred million; to authorize the Government of Canada to underwrite the issue of shares of the Corporation, and at its discretion to invest in shares of the Corporation on its own account not exceeding in number ten per cent of the total number of issued and outstanding shares of the Corporation, the amount of which underwriting commitment, together with the total amount invested by the Government of Canada in shares of the Corporation, shall not exceed two hundred and fifty million dollars; to authorize the Government of Canada to make loans to or purchase debentures of the Corporation to an aggregate amount not exceeding one hundred million dollars and to sell to the Corporation the holdings of Canada of shares of certain Crown corporations; and to provide further for other necessary and incidental matters relating to the establishment of the Corporation, its objects and powers, and its management, operation and control.

Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
I was preparing to give the following information on this subject today. The Point Edward Naval Base, Nova Scotia, is being transferred to the Department of Transport, which will continue to operate the Coast Guard school now located there. The naval service stores operation will be discontinued when the space which it now occupies adjacent to the jetty is required for industrial development.
The Department of Transport, with the Industrial Estates Corporation of the Province of Nova Scotia, is working out arrangements under which Canadian Motor Industries Limited will establish a plant at this location and provide for other industrial development. Employment will be created for approximately 500 by the initial industrial development, and employment for considerably larger numbers is expected in the future.
The Department of National Defence now has a stall of approximately 243 at the base for its storage operations and for maintenance and servicing of the base. Some of this staff will be transferred to the Department of Transport which will assume responsibility for maintenance and servicing formerly done by the Department of National Defence. Arrangements have been worked out by the Department of National Defence and the Department of Labour to ensure that employment opportunities as they are created by the industrial development will be available to the remaining staff, and that the rundown of the national defence activities is timed to fit in with the availability of new jobs.
In view of these arrangements, alternative employment opportunities will become available for those now employed at the naval base and, in addition, it is expected that many new jobs will develop for others in the area.

As a matter of fact, I think the head of the Globe and Mail bureau in Ottawa, George
April 28. 1985

Bain, wrote a very humorous column this morning, in which he referred to the fact that a married man with two dependants under these income tax savings would save $3 a year. Mr. Speaker, because I know many hon. Members want to speak in this debate and that time is circumscribed, I wish only to speak to some of the highlights. If I may now deal with the figures in the green book, there are roughly 3,300,000 Canadian taxpayers whose income is $5,000 or less, representing not quite three quarters of all taxpayers in Canada. There are 20,700, odd, income tax payers in Canada whose taxable income is over $25,000, and their savings, of course, will be much larger. They can possibly contribute to the development of the economy, and I realize that the Minister prayed the other night that their savings would be directed toward that end. But these people who have incomes of $20,000, $25,000, or $30,000 and over have already bought their refrigerators and washing machines. They are going to use this money for investment or, probably more to the point-and I do not blame them one bit-they will use it for a trip to Spain, or be able to spend two more weeks in Spain than they otherwise would have spent had these tax deductions not been made. So, as I say, the argument that these tax cuts will increase consumption does not, I think, bear analysis.
As a matter of fact, as far as these tax cuts are concerned this budget gives the least relief to those who need it the most. It gives the most to those who need it the least, and any contribution to an expanding economy is absolutely and completely infinitesimal. I think that is a fair summary, in general. I do not expect the Minister to agree with that wholeheartedly, but I do not think he can help but admit that generally that is the situation with respect to these tax cuts.
There is one specific matter, Mr. Speaker, to which I want to make reference and which was not included in the budget speech. I dealt with it briefly the other night and I want to emphasize it again this afternoon. I am referring to the failure of the Minister to deal in any way whatever with the sales tax on machinery and equipment entering
698	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan into production. Virtually everybody in this country agrees-I am sure some of the Minister's colleagues must have had some heated arguments with him about this, and certainly the financial press editors have urged this in every way possible-that it is necessary to reduce our costs and maintain efficiency. In fact, the report of the Economic Council says just that.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
This statement has been made by every financial writer in Canada. In spite of this fact, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has failed completely to deal with this matter in any way, shape or form, and one cannot help being driven to the opinion, the judgment or conclusion that he has taken this position because he is sensitive about this matter as a result of the many changes and retreats he has had to make in respect of budgets brought down in the past. He has now taken a firm position and has maintained the sales tax on equipment and machinery for production.
I am not now dealing with the sales tax on building materials, although I intend to say something about that at a later stage. Certainly it is the prerogative of the Minister to adopt the position he has taken in this regard and I would not be too critical of him, although I think he may have been in error. However, in spite of his prerogative regarding the sales tax on building materials and his decision not to remove that tax, irrespective of the substantial number of representations made, there is no reasonable excuse for the Minister's failure to remove the sales tax on equipment and machinery for production.
As I have said, one could quote from many documents and articles in this regard, because numerous arguments have been advanced by many competent authorities in Canada, as well as by some incompetent ones I suspect, which have urged the Minister to make this tax cut. I should like to quote from one of these many articles, and I have in my hand a pamphlet published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association under the heading "Industry". This is the April publication of this pamphlet.
While I realize that the Minister may not agree with this article and will say, as perhaps will many others, that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association is prejudiced and biased and looking after its own interests, if it is read in conjunction with the many other similar articles that have been published,

it will be appreciated that the secondary industry-the manufacturing industry must be developed and increased. We have been exporting primary products for a great many years, and we will continue to do so I hope at an accelerated rate; but the Canadian economy and those young people who sit in our galleries from time to time and look down upon us wondering what we are going to do with respect to their future depend to a great extent on the expansion of manufactured goods. For those reasons I make no apology whatever in reading from this pamphlet produced by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association under the heading "Industry".
This pamphlet is the April, 1965 issue and I should like to read two paragraphs as follows:
New manufacturing investment in the Canadian economy in 1965 is forecast to exceed $2.2 billion, a sum never before equalled in a single year. It is 23 per cent greater than the $1.8 billion invested last year and two-thirds as much again as the $1.3 billion of 1963.
That is an expectation, or a forecast, and it is followed later in the article by a qualifying paragraph which reads as follows:
Rightly or wrongly, it is industry's expectation that Mr. Gordon in his forthcoming budget will cut both corporate and personal tax rates, and scrap altogether the absurd, cost-inflating sales tax on production machinery and equipment. Should these expectations not be realized, there could very well be a distinct scaling down in capital investment intentions to the detriment of the economy and government revenues alike.
I am sure most hon. Members have read statements by the President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, dealing with this budget, which appeared in several newspapers today. We recognize the fact that Mr. Cumming is speaking from a manufacturer's point of view and no doubt is swayed because of that fact. The Minister can deprecate these statements to any extent he sees fit, but the fact remains that Canadian manufacturers represent one of the keystones of the Canadian economy. Manufacturing in Canada is one of the great foundation stones upon which our economy must be based, and it must be encouraged to grow and grow.
The President of that Association is reported in today's issue of the business and finance section of the Montreal Gazette as having said:
From the manufacturing industry's point of view, it's a damp squib budget-
He also is reported as having said:
The producer, the mainspring of the national economy, remains overtaxed.

The article then states:
Mr. Cumming also attacked Mr. Gordon's failure to remove the 11 per cent tax on machinery and equipment.
This failure is "a major let-down and a serious error in judgment"-
The article then refers to corporate tax rates to which I will make a passing reference in a moment.
On the evening before last when I was dealing with this matter I referred to a statement made by the President of Chemcell to its annual meeting on April 20, 1965. The import of that statement was that this tax on production machinery and equipment should be removed. In part it reads as follows:
This tax is a serious brake on national progress. Industry is temporarily encouraged through various tax incentives to embark on capital expenditure programs, while at the same time it is burdened with an 11 per cent tax on production machinery and equipment which cuts down on its ability to compete with foreign producers. These two situations are to say the least not compatible. Only the general level of Canadian prosperity has concealed the innate viciousness of this tax, and when the economy weakens, we in Canada may well have lost our ability to compete.
The next sentence is the one I quoted the evening before last, Mr. Speaker, and is:
Chemcell will pay in 1965 over one million dollars as a surcharge on capital if this tax is not removed.
The tax has not been removed and I suggest -and I will deal with this aspect a little more fully before I conclude-that it would be better for the Minister to deal with a tax such as this than to deal with a general tax reduction across the board. One tax is related to personal income tax while the other is related to industrial and economical development.
In round figures the Minister has suggested that as a result of this general across-the-board tax reduction $170 million will be left in the hands of Canadian consumers. This will happen as a result of the saving to individual taxpayers. The amount will vary depending upon income and I would not want to suggest how much you will save, Mr. Speaker.

such action would be an impingement upon provincial rights with regard to education. The Provinces would have free scope. The only thing they would have to do would be to spend at least as much money on education as they are now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always approach the budgets of my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) with lively interest because one never knows quite where he is going to lead one, or which way he is going to jump. I feel it might not be inappropriate to suggest that he moves in a mysterious way his wonders to perform, but we are not quite sure what these wonders are that he wishes to perform.
After a great deal of advance publicity-in fact I may say the publicity rather outdid the actual turn when it came on the stage- we were told he is going to cut taxes 10 per cent across the board and this is going to have a dynamic effect on our economy.
I have just been wondering what the purpose of this tax cut could have been. It can hardly have been to afford relief to those in our society who require it most, because in that event he would have put his tax cuts in the lower income groups. He would perhaps have raised the exemption level. Instead he left it as it is at present where, for instance, a young married man with two children, living on $3,000 a year, is given a tax cut of $3 a year and still pays $26 a year.
Now, $26 a year is probably quite important to a young couple in that position. In fact I know it is, yet at the same time the man who gets ten times that amount, $30,000, is to be given a tax relief of $600. What for? Why is he to get a tax relief of $600? Why are you and I, Mr. Speaker, to get tax reliefs when still the man on $3,000 a year is going to have to dig in his pocket for $26 a year which he can ill afford?
Therefore it cannot really have been for the relief of those who need it most that the Minister of Finance has made his tax cut in this form. Then we are told, of course, that the main purpose is to stimulate consumption, to stimulate purchasing power and thereby give a shot in the arm to the economy, if it needs it.
Again I wonder how the Minister of Finance thought he was going to do that through this particular method of tax cuts because, as the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), who preceded me, pointed out, the man with $30,000 income has probably got his refrigerator by now, and probably his wife has a fur coat too, and it will probably result in his taking an extra two weeks in Spain or Florida with this unexpected windfall from the generous Minister of Finance.

Nor can it be that these tax cuts were made with the idea of moving toward some sort of equalization of incomes, because again I point out what happens is that those who need it least get most, and those who need it most get least. We who are in the $12,000 a year and up income tax bracket for tax purposes will get a somewhere around $150 and up tax cut. It is very nice and I am sure we are very grateful to the Minister, but I suggest to him that the price is too high if in order to have that it has been necessary to deduct from the very meagre incomes of those in the lower brackets just a little more of what they have earned than is necessary, o (4:10 p.m.)
I should have liked the Minister to raise exemption levels. I see no reason for his not having done so, because this would have met all the expressed objectives of these tax cuts. When they are all boiled down and when we take into consideration the effect of the contributions to the Canada Pension Plan, the dynamic economic effects of these tax cuts will, I suggest, be precisely nil. They will be completely unnoticeable and a complete waste of time from that point of view. They will simply have created and developed still more inequities in our society.
While I am on my feet I may perhaps say something which will make me unpopular with a lot of people. It has to do with our whole attitude toward taxes. I have noticed in the course of a long life laid waste in getting and spending that by and large the dollar I spend for taxes gets me a better bargain than the other money I expend. Of course, it is the "done" thing to growl about taxes, and for this reason whenever a Minister of Finance announces a tax cut he stands with a smirk of conscious virtue; he waits the grateful applause, and the applause comes. It all seems to me somewhat illogical-the grateful applauders might well have hesitated in an attempt to find out just what they were applauding. Because even in the hands of the most incompetent Government I maintain that what we get for our tax dollar is a better bargain than what we get individually. That is true even of this Government which has opened up new and unheard of vistas of incompetence and bungling.
There are people in our community to whom this does not apply. The rich have no need of the amenities which are provided by tax dollars. They do not have to worry about a proper medicare service being provided for citizens of this country, should that ever come
April 28, 1965
about. They do not have to bother very much about the public school system for the education of their children. They have a vested interest in the reduction of taxes. However, I suggest that those of us who are not rich have a vested interest in seeing that the total of the amenities of our country is continuously increased and that for our tax dollar we get a more comfortable life, a more worth-while life and a more satisfactory society in which to live. So I have no bouquets for the Minister with regard to his tax cut. In any event it is an ineffective one; it will do nothing of consequence apart from annoying a lot of people who find that their reduction amounts to only $3, though it will amount to $600 in respect of men earning ten times their income. Added to this will be the knowledge that the present Government is not likely to move ahead very rapidly in the field of supplying services and amenities and improving the whole quality of life in our society.
Another item in the budget which created a great deal of interest was the Canada Development Corporation proposal. Here again it has been suggested that the Minister stole some of the laundry from the Socialist washline. Perhaps this is the impression which it was intended to convey. Certainly it took in the Toronto Globe and Mail, because they actually imagine this measure amounted to Socialism by the back door. I would think that had they gone into the New York Stock Exchange they would have found out what it really is, which is, of course, the New York Stock Exchange version of peoples' capitalism. What Members opposite did steal, as is so often the case, was the name. But added to the name was a different idea.
The reason is not far to seek. Contrary to the general impression, the Liberal Party is a doctrinaire Party. Usually we Socialists are accused of being doctrinaire. But the Liberal Party is the most doctrinaire Party in the country because it applies one yardstick to every proposal, that is, it must fall within the confines of what is politely known as free enterprise; everything must be fitted to this Procurstean bed. They may deck their proposals out in semi-Socialist or progressive clothing but in the final analysis they must fit this doctrine which is rigid and unchanging. At the present time we see the Liberal Government taking this idea of a Development Corporation and fitting it into its doctrinaire pattern, proving once more what is the essential philosophy of the Liberal Party. This philosophy is that the main purpose of human 22620-451
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron society is to provide opportunities for the more acquisitive members of that society to profit by the operation of a modern economy, and that everything else must be subservient to this idea.
The idea which animated most of us who invented the original name was that this would be another tool in the hands of the Government to stimulate the expansion of the Canadian economy. What have we got? We find ourselves with just a vast mutual investment trust, in no way differing from those which are already in existence except that you and I and the other citizens of Canada will be asked to sponsor it; we shall be given the chance to invest in it to the modest degree of $100 million, or 10 per cent. We shall also be asked to stand by with the buckets to bail this Corporation out of trouble, if necessary, to buy its bonds when needed, and so on. But we are not going to control it. In fact, the Minister says plainly that this Corporation will stand on its own feet free from Government control. If this is what the Globe and Mail calls Socialism by the back door I think its editors have a lot to learn.
I notice that at one point the Minister suggested that this Corporation would be expected to invest its funds in such a way as to serve the best interests of the Canadian economy. It would be "expected" to do this. He did not tell the house it would be made to do so. I suppose he pictures himself as a latter day Lord Nelson standing on the quarterdeck and giving the signal "England expects that every man will do his duty". You know, I think he is really more in the guise of Captain Morgan raising the Jolly Roger and beckoning all the buccaneers to climb aboard this richly laden merchant vessel, all ready to loot. And they will come vaulting over singing "Yo, ho, ho and a bottle of rum" because they are never slow in recognizing a proposition which is in their own interest.

I do not think we can be so naive as that. And once they have got control of the directorate, what will be their purpose? It will be the purpose of the directorate of all private Corporations, a perfectly legitimate one under these terms of reference, of maximizing profits at all costs, and any idea that this is a new deal to develop the Canadian economy goes by the board.
It is, again, a demonstration of the unspoken but firmly held conviction of Liberal Governments that the directors of insurance companies, the banks and trust companies are really better fitted to manage the country's affairs than those who have been chosen by the people, and that the Government's role is mainly that of handmaiden to serve the interests of private business. In fact, Mr. Speaker, as I read the description of this new company I was reminded of a definition of a politician that one of my colleagues in the British Columbia House gave many years ago, and I think it is very appropriate on this occasion; that the politician is the man who climbs the tree to shake the fruit down to the hogs below.
In fact, the idea that this is going to help the Canadian people, that this is designed to serve the interests of Canada, is blown sky high when we come to the suggestion that we are going to sell Polymer to them. Why are we going to sell Polymer to this Corporation? You and I, Mr. Speaker, are both share holders, very small ones-we hold about one-nineteen-millionth of the shares of the Polymer Corporation-and why is the Minister going to sell our property to a few people in Canada, when it now belongs to all of us? In what way is this going to stimulate the development of the Canadian economy? How is this going to improve matters for the economy of Canada? Why should these funds be invested in a concern that has already established a reputation for outstanding success and competence and efficiency? Why should funds be diverted there, when the Minister tells us that his purpose in establishing this Canada Development Corporation is to create an instrument for the development of the Canadian economy? This, I think, is just another demonstration of the fact that the Liberal Party has no faith in its own Members; that the Liberal Government has no faith in its own Members. Of course, I can understand their reluctance to place faith


in themselves, but on the other hand I am equally reluctant to place the faith that they place and that the Minister places in the hands of those who now control our financial institutions.
Having dealt with the Canada Development Corporation, Mr. Speaker, let us turn to some other aspects of the Budget and just see how well the Minister has done. I noted again this time that the Minister made his customary obeisance to the myths of the unqualified virtues of a balanced budget. I felt, I suppose, like some of those Christian missionaries used to feel when they found a native they thought they had converted to Christendom going out again and bowing down to the old tribal gods. Here the Minister does it again. He seems to suggest, again, that this is the summum bonum of national financing. He tells us we have brought the economy under control; we have now set our house in order. But have we? Is our house in order when we have 3.9 per cent unemployed; when slums disgrace every major centre in the Dominion of Canada; when education is in a crisis; when whole areas are, and have been for decades, in a depressed condition? Is this setting our house in order?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And with the farmers' delegation coming in.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and with the farmers' delegation roaming through the buildings? The Minister tells us that everything is wonderful. In fact, he stands up and, as Ministers of Finance always do, takes great credit for the fact that the Canadian economy at the present time is in a prosperous condition. I am always diverted by the manner in which Ministers do this. Whenever things are prosperous, then it is the result of the wisdom and sagacity of the Government; and when things go wrong, of course, it is an act of God. God is elbowed out of the way very quickly, though, when there is an upturn. He is allowed to be responsible for disasters, but not for benefactions.
The Minister tells us we are riding the crest of a boom; but what does he do about it? Does he do anything about these things that are staring us in the face, the squalour that lies behind much of our affluent society's fagade today? He boasts about the fact that he is bringing his budget almost into balance, that the debits and the credits are lying down together; but he does not do anything about the means with which to cope with these disease spots in our economy. What
April 28. 1965

does he do? He cuts a few taxes to make us forget the squalour. He establishes a vast private enterprise under Government sponsorship, and he leaves these other things untouched and uncorrected.
Let us turn to one of the matters in which we lag very far behind in Canada. On this occasion the Toronto Globe and Mail perhaps did a better job than it did when it characterized the Canada Development Corporation as a Socialist measure. This is a report of a speech made by Dr. Frank Forward as director of the Science Secretariat to the Privy Council, which was given to a number of Canadian researchers some few weeks ago. This article was published on April 3 this year, and it has this to say:
The problem is not that the Medical Research Council has decided to cut back on grants. It hasn't. In fact, it has increased its total amount of funds by about one-third over last year's. The increase is just not enough.
One precipitating factor in today's dilemma was the United States' decision to reduce its grants through its Public Health and National Institutes of Health to developed countries.
We had, of course, been living on our American friends' generosity, and when they decided they could not afford it any more, we found that the Canadian Government had nothing to put in its place. The article continues:
It is a question of policy, too-federal Government policy on science, or rather, the lack of it. Despite much talk and the appointment last May of Dr. Frank Forward.. .the Canadian Government still has no well-defined national goals in science.
Dr. Forward revealed this regrettable lack of direction and resolve a few weeks ago in an address to the Canadian Society for Clinical Investigation.
It says further:
It was not an easy audience for Dr. Forward to address. They were what their president described as a group of angry young men. And they were angry because, in the words of Dr. D. V. Bates of McGill University: "The Canadian Government has been worse served in its scientific research advice in the last six or seven years than any other Western government". They had at their fingertips a wealth of arguments and statistics to show their guests (Trade and Commerce Minister Mitchell Sharp attended the dinner as the Cabinet's representative) that, as a consequence, Canadian universities had inadequate facilities and vacant staff positions.
.. .Dr. Forward told them precisely what they did not believe and what they did not want to hear. After prefacing his remarks with the tantalizing caveat that if he were still in university he could "get up and say what I damn well thought", he claimed that there was no brain drain and that Canada s research funds were just about adequate for a country of her size...
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron
Strangely enough. Dr. Forward himself once seemed to understand the situation. The lack of exciting research opportunities, he said, had deprived Canada of too many native scientists who had emigrated to the United States. "It's not just a matter of higher salaries over there", he said. "I know several brilliant researchers who would gladly come back to this country, for less money if necessary, providing we could offer the challenge and the stimulation".
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I have been approached by young scientists in the Government service who tell me of their disquiet and uneasiness over the failure of the Government to tackle the problem of scientific research. They point out that one of the necessary factors in scientific research is size. In the United States, for instance, there are five what are known as research parks in which there has been a concerted and integrated effort both by government and industry to develop a research centre which will attract first-class research brains, people who can go there and have the stimulating effect of exchanging their ideas with those of their colleagues. Here in Canada we have had nothing done by the Government to solve this problem.
I have here a letter written by the General Secretary of the Canadian Medical Association to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh). Dr. Kelly has this to say:
We agree with the dictum of the Royal Commission that the education of physicians is a matter of national concern and, despite the constitutional complexities which are inherent, we ask that the Government of Canada recognize this and express its concern by making very substantial funds available for purposes of medical education and medical research. Education and research in our field of interest are so intimately related that they should be regarded as inseparable in the current context.
Let me also quote from a letter written by the physician-in-chief of the Royal Victoria Hospital, who is also director of the McGill University Clinic at McGill University. He
says:
I will be pleased to hear of your progress In calling this to the attention of the Government.
That is the lack of research facilities.
I think Canadian biological research is at the crossroads and that our present position is entirely dependant upon the Government's lack of recognition of the problem. Either we become a second, third, or even fourth rate nation with respect to contributions to biological research or we must have relief. I think government is near sighted in recognizing that if it doesn't have teachers and individuals guiding the clinical care of patients, who are also investigators, the level of competence of our graduates from medical school
706	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron [DOT]will gradually fall and the over-all level of medical care throughout our nation will become increasingly poor.
These are expressions of opinion from people who are experts in the field. Yet the Government bring in a budget which makes not the slightest provision to correct this situation. All they do is do a snow job on the people of Canada to try and make them believe that real research facilities are being established and that real research programs are being carried out. In fact no real effort is being made to do this. Instead, the Minister of Finance comes before us and smirks modestly that he has almost balanced the Budget. He tells us we are riding a wave of prosperity. He tells us that everything is lovely today in our Canadian garden under the aegis of the great Liberal Party. Yet in these most vital areas of national development today this Government is doing precisely nothing and has exhibited not the slightest intention of doing anything. Yet we are asked to applaud the Minister when he comes before us with his budget.
I suggested last year, Mr. Speaker, that we had at least progressed to the point where it was understood that a budget is more than merely a statement of the housekeeping expenses of the Government. We had advanced to the point where we realized that a budget is a mechanism by which a Government, if it is active, alert and intelligent, will direct and guide the development of the economy, will sponsor those areas which need help, will see that the economy expands and that the distribution of national income is not too inequitable.
I suggest now, Mr. Speaker, that we have something else to face as well. I suggested at that time there was something else which the Government had to do, and that was to take into consideration the quality of life in our society. I was very much struck by the report of the Economic Council for Canada when they tell us that we are going to require one and a half million jobs by 1970. But they do not tell us what kind of jobs. They do not tell us what sort of jobs these people are going to occupy. They do not tell us what sort of things will be achieved by these jobs. They do not tell us whether this is going to improve the nation of Canada or whether it is not. They do not tell us what sort of lives these one and a half million job holders will be condemned to. These are questions which now have to be faced by modern governments, because they surround the whole question of the quality of life in our national community.

DEBATES	April 28, 1965
It is not enough for the Government to come before us and say that our gross national product has expanded immeasurably and this year will reach $48 billion. Statistically this sounds very wonderful; but I suggest that sometimes our statisticians and economists should take a drive through the slum districts of the principal cities of Canada, that they should examine the sort of lives lived today by 25 per cent of our people, people who, experts tell us, are living at or near the poverty line. Then we could put this whole business of gross national product and economics into its proper perspective and realize that governments have to do more than merely stimulate the economy and make it expand; they must also decide in what way the economy will expand and what sort of quality of lives the people in our society are going to live.
We hear a great deal these days about revolutions, and many revolutions are in fact taking place-technological revolutions, political revolutions-and most of the time we consider revolutions within that framework. But I suggest that there is another revolution going on today, perhaps a more serious one, certainly one that is more difficult to discern and to define. It is a revolution in the ideas of men, a revolution in the sense of values of people in our modern, affluent society. In our naivete we used to imagine that most of our problems would be solved, once we had solved all the physical problems of life, such as giving everybody a good job, making sure they had a satisfactory income, a good place to live, and consequently the new Jerusalem would arrive on time. These things are all important, and I consider that in light of the wealthy economy that is Canada's the existence of some of the things I have outlined today is nothing but an indication of sluttish housekeeping, of which we should be thoroughly ashamed. We should not tolerate it for another moment because we are too rich and wealthy to tolerate, with good conscience, this sort of thing.
But having done that we will have to face this other revolution, and it is beginning to make itself felt in our society today in rather disturbing ways. For example, it is making itself felt among our young people, in some cases in an encouraging manner. I read and heard a lot of critical comment about the young people who took part in the recent demonstrations in front of this House, in front of the American Embassy in Toronto, and at various places and for various causes. Whatever we think about the value of the causes
April 28, 1965

or the wisdom of the method of conveying their protests, nevertheless these young people were expressing a concern for the human race which went beyond their own individual welfare and individual satisfaction. I think this is an indication of one part of this revolution which is taking place in the thinking of men.
The other part is not so encouraging. There are the continued outbreaks of senseless violence against people who are unknown to the young people concerned. Groups of young thugs go about beating up people for no conceivable reason, which again is an expression of dissatisfaction with the sort of society we have provided for them. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is not much that you and I and those of our generation, and younger, can do about this in the way of direction. We cannot tell this rising generation what sort of values they should have; they have to work them out for themselves. What we can do is give them the intellectual tools by which they can work out a new scale of values that will be more satisfying to them than the scale of values of the present affluent society.
I hope that before too long Governments in advanced countries such as Canada will take into account this terrible need which now lies before us of providing a more satisfactory life for people who have become disillusioned with an affluent society. This will require immense investment in education. I agree with the hon. Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) that we must not allow constitutional barriers to interfere in this regard because this is something too serious to allow legalities to stand in the way.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I do not think we can solve this problem merely by providing funds for higher education in the way we have been providing them to date, because much of the failure in respect of Canadian education occurs at an earlier period of time when ill-trained teachers in schools with classes far too large attempt to cope with an impossible situation. Somehow we must deal with this problem and divert to education the vast funds which are now being drained from the Canadian economy.
Perhaps when our young people who protest in one way or another have succeeded in establishing new values we shall then have not merely a prosperous Canada, but a civilized Canada in which people will be able to live lives more satisfying, pleasurable and useful than they are now living.
The Budget-Mr. Leboe
I now wish to make more precise the amendment advanced by the Official Opposition. I move, seconded by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the words "lower income groups" and by inserting instead thereof the following words:
"by exempting from income tax all single persons with incomes up to $1,500 a year and all married persons with incomes up to $3,000 a year, and by failing to raise the old age security pension to $100 a month".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In the very short time available to me I should first like to address my remarks to the budget as it relates to the fiscal and monetary policies of the Provinces of Canada.
I think it most important that we recognize the fact that the Provinces of Canada are the custodians of our natural resources, and that as custodians of our natural resources the policies of provincial Governments have more effect on the economic life of Canada and its prosperity than Federal Government policies.
With this fact in mind I should like to refer briefly to the May 1, 1965 edition of Maclean's magazine, as it bears out exactly the position I have advanced in respect of provincial Government policy and the relationship of these fiscal policies to Canada's prosperity.
The article in this magazine to which I refer is headed "Anybody can have a boom-but B.C.'s got three". The introductory paragraph reads:
Two mighty rivers, a flock of new mines and a billion or so trees are making British Columbia the fast-buck centre of Canada. But the most wondrous natural resources of all are Mr. Bennett, who runs the place, and the array of coast-style go-getters who have learned to prosper without the blessing of eastern financiers.
The boom that is taking place in British Columbia is one that commenced quite recently. It is a boom that is affecting the whole economic life of Canada. Approximately $1 billion worth of goods have been bought by British Columbia from Ontario and Quebec alone in the last 12 months. When the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec refer to the economic conditions that exist in those provinces they should look westward to the boom taking place in Western Canada with thankfulness because herein lies the secret of their success.

DEBATES	April 28, 1965
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Early in his budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) referred to the balance of payments, and certain words in this connection caught my attention. He said that the improvement in the balance of payments had been achieved "not by restricting imports and travel by Canadians". If this is so, why have we not relaxed the regulations with regard to the total value of the goods that Canadians can bring back to Canada from the United States or other countries? Why can we not bring about a situation whereby our people can bring in more goods and services duty free, if it is not going to affect our balance of payments?
I have had numerous requests, as every Member of the House has, that consideration be given to raising the total value of goods that can be brought back to Canada by Canadians returning from other countries. According to the statement made by the Minister in the budget, this is not affecting the balance of payments. Therefore I am surprised that the Minister has not done something about this matter because he must have had representations made to him just as you and I have, Mr. Speaker. If we are to encourage free and easy travel between Canada and the United States and other countries, and if we expect the people of these other countries to visit Canada, certainly this is one avenue that should be explored to bring about a better relationship between different countries. People visit Canada and spend money in our country, and they will expect us to treat them as well as we are treated when we travel abroad.
The Minister also stated in his Budget speech that capital must be found to carry out economic expansion both for business and for government. I should like to ask the Minister this question: What is capital? I know he can give me the answer. I have said before and I say again I have never seen money grow on bushes in my life, and if it is money we are short of I say that a dollar brought into being by our central bank will be just as effective in doing business as a dollar that is imported from some other bank that is financing a prospectus. If we want industrial expansion, then I say that when we revise the Bank Act we should give the banks a little more leeway. Let us give them the opportunity to enter into the mortgage field by lending on fixed assets.
We know that today the expansion of credit is largely confined to the terms of section 88
April 28, 1965	COMMONS
of the Bank Act. Surely there is room for the banks as Canadian institutions to supply some of the financing for industry on the basis of taking chattel mortgages on certain fixed assets. It is no secret that an individual may have a very great potential with regard to dealing with a natural resource, but Canadian banks under the law are not in a position to provide the type of service that is required for that individual to go ahead with his expansion program. He has to pay higher interest rates on money he has raised from other secondary sources. This hampers the individual and hampers the industrial expansion of Canada. It hampers the material growth of the nation. It hampers trade patterns. The result is that we find ourselves in the position of having many more foreign owned industries in Canada than we would have if the banks, after their charters are reviewed, were given more freedom by being granted the power to accept mortgages.
Before five o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to the fact that so far as I can see the Economic Council of Canada in its report failed absolutely to make reference to Provincial fiscal policy and industrial expansion in the Provinces. It seems to me that there lies the very foundation of our society. This is where we must start if we are going to create a million and a half jobs within a certain period of time. This is where we must look to find out exactly where we are going. But in the review of the Economic Council of Canada we find nothing regarding the effect of Provincial policies on the economic life of Canada. I should like to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact it is five o'clock, and adjourn the debate.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kooienay West) moved:
subtopic: SUGGESTED CREATION OF POLLUTION CONTROL DIVISION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of the creation of a Water Pollution Control Division, composed of representatives of the 10 provinces, within the framework of the proposed National Resources Council, with powers and funds required to institute research programs, collect, collate, and analyse water control data, and to co-ordinate the water pollution control objectives for the provinces; in addition, to further the study of water pollution control problems of a national character.
DEBATES	709
Proposed Water Pollution Control [DOT] (5 :00 p.m.)
He said: Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the topic which I wish to discuss for a few minutes this afternoon I want to say how much this group welcomes the hundreds of farmers who came to Ottawa today to lay their complaints before the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) and the Government. I do that because I have great sympathy for their cause. I am actually one of the few hillbillies left in Canada. I farm in the mountains of Kootenay West, in the Selkirk range, and am more acquainted with grub hoes, cross-cut saws and pickaxes than farmers on the prairies. I am very glad the farmers are taking this aggressive and militant action in presenting their views to the Minister, and I am sure their talks with him and with other members of Parliament will bear fruit in the days ahead.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are surrounded by and we are part of the eternal flux of life in an environment of natural forces, particularly when we come to deal with the question of water pollution and its increasing effect on mankind. An Eastern proverb states:
To survive all men must hold hands, and all living things are kin in the wholeness of nature.
Any wrong which nature may commit she has centuries to repair, but we whose days are short-and some of us are very conscious of that fact-must walk warily lest we become the victims of the wasteland we are rapidly making in Canada under present circumstances.
Water is Canada's most important natural resource. It must be clear to all those who have studied this problem that a national water management policy is a priority which must continue to concern all governments in Canada, all organizations interested in this problem and the people of Canada generally.
Before proceeding I wish to pay tribute to the good work that has been undertaken to date, with limited resources, by the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission, particularly with respect to the St. Lawrence Seaway and some other waterways. I want also to pay my tribute to the personnel of the water resource divisions of the national and provincial governments which, from our point of view, have had very limited budgets to deal with the problem that faces us at this time. I also want to pay tribute to all those public organizations interested in the conservation of all our renewable natural resources.
April 28. 1965

Proposed Water Pollution Control
Further, I willingly pay tribute to that section of the press that is interested in reporting what is done in this Parliament and various other Legislatures to meet this problem. Some sections of the press would rather deal with the divorce problems of a Hollywood star, but we do have some solid people in the Press Gallery and throughout the press of this country, who realize how important it is to inform the Canadian people on this question. I particularly wish to mention Mr. J. S. Cram of the Family Herald, whose articles on the subject have done a great deal to inform a wide section of the public, particularly the farming public, on this question of vital importance.
I must also say I am particularly pleased with the actions taken to date by the Canadian Council of Resource Ministers and its determination in recent months to pay particular attention to the problems of air, soil and water pollution. Once again I have no hesitation in mentioning the former Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the hon. Member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), for the progressive approach he took to this situation and for all the work he did in bringing that conference into being in Montreal.
This is a problem that affects all of Canada. It is a problem on the St. Lawrence, on the Great Lakes, on our lakes and rivers across the country which are close to large centres of population, and I am very sorry to say we now have the problem developing in Kootenay West, which is the constituency I have the honour to represent. To date we have been pretty fortunate in that the Columbia and Kootenay Rivers, and all the lakes in that part of Southeastern B.C., are practically unpolluted, but there is a danger because of increased population in certain areas and of industrial expansion that pollution will proceed at a much increased rate in the years ahead.
In that connection I want to quote from the Nelson Daily News of September 14, 1964, a report headed, "Cady Call for Attack on Pollution Supported," meaning supported by the municipalities of Kootenay district:
Commissioner Cady felt the task should be given to the National Research Council or some other allied group.
That is the purpose of the resolution we have before us this afternoon.
"We are slowly losing one of our greatest resources-water-and industry has already heard this warning and has got the message," he said.
[Mr. Herridge.l
"So far as municipalities are concerned," Mr. Cady stated, "They are unable to correct the situation without aid."
He also said:
A systematic plan of attack upon pollution should be devised and government sources should
provide the necessary resources____"The day is
coming when we can't go to the kitchen tap and draw a glassful of uncontaminated water. We must do better than that."
I might mention in passing that Mr. Cady has been nominated as the Liberal opponent of the N.D.P. candidate who will be nominated to contest the next election in Kootenay West, but I give him credit for his interest in this problem. I forgot to mention that he also had a little go at Mr. Bennett and stated:
If Premier Bennett can lend the province of Quebec $100 million to finance their projects it ought to be possible for the provincial government to provide low cost loans to municipalities for financing their share of pollution control costs.
The districts particularly concerned in my constituency are the City of Nelson, the City of Trail and the villages of Castlegar and Kinnaird, and Mr. Cady has urged that Premier Bennett provide these municipalities with low-cost loans.
I have drafted out what I think a water control division should give consideration to, and I would be very happy to hear suggestions from other hon. Members. I suggest a water pollution control division should undertake the following research and development program, as a possible nucleus for continued research to meet the problems that arise from changing living habits, new industrial techniques and continued urban, agricultural and industrial expansion:
1.	Establish engineering parameters which will continuously assess the total pollution and the actual state of our water resources. That is essential because then we would be informed on the problem with which we are going to deal.
2.	Probe for new methods of waste treatment geared to remove any and all contaminants. There is a great field for research here.
3.	Evaluate the health and economic aspects to crystallize public opinion and establish a basis for a national policy, which would be worked out in co-operation with the provincial governments.
4.	Develop adequate hydrologic, geologic and geographic data, co-ordinating these data into a nation-wide scheme, making inventory of our total water resources using drillers' reports and other data.
April 28, 1985
5.	Set up a comprehensive watershed research program to learn the effects of logging, farming, recreation, construction and other activities on the quality of water.
6.	Collect reliable basic data on water usage by industry and by region from coast to coast, including a detailed survey of selected industries.
7.	Investigate the individual and composite effects of the many complex substances that are polluting air and water. This includes a study of agricultural chemicals and how these are handled, suractants such as alkyl benzene sulfonate, phenols, cyanides, and others. The studies should be concerned with the methods of treatment and the establishing of safe limits under continuous exposure.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
8.	The division might further evaluate the effect of suspended solids on benthic organisms in conjunction with such United States workers as Hoak of the Mellon Institute who has done a great deal of valuable work in this field and, in so doing, set rational limits to pollution of this type.
9.	They might set up a program for monitoring and releasing radioactive wastes; measure alpha and beta radiation for both suspended and dissolved solids and then determine better treatment methods; determine the safe levels for aquatic life by finding the concentration factors of the critical radioisotopes; organs or tissue which accumulate radioactivity; the most sensitive stages in the lives of marine biology; the method by which organisms assimilate radioactive materials. This is a field about which we must be more concerned than we have been in the past.
10.	They could evaluate oxidation stabilization ponds particularly for various Canadian regions; establish their effects on groundwater; establish their effect on pathogenic bacteria and viruses; establish reliable design criteria and especially ascertain the design relationships between B.O.D. loading, volume, depth and desired degree of treatment. Establish any other limitations such as types of wastes.
11.	Establish the inactivation of pathogenic organisms that is obtained by all the modern recognized methods of treating sewage and handling sludge; determine the minimum disinfection required for each method. This is very necessary for smaller communities and villages which cannot undertake large expenditures.
12.	It could study the travel of pathogenic bacteria and viruses in the water tables and
711
Proposed Water Pollution Control in various formations. It is interesting to note how these viruses travel through soil formations and how pollution is found in water a long distance from where the pollution originally occurred.
13.	It could obtain full data on areas using septic tanks; methods of construction, laying of tile, proximity to wells and the effects on these wells.
14.	It could assist industry in the study of its problems, realizing that many industrial waste problems are highly complex and may require a combination of industrial and sanitary engineering skills.
15.	Conduct oceanography studies as related to waste disposal, including a study of salt water intrusion into groundwater resources. This is of particular interest to communities close to tidewater.
16.	Establish the purification capacity and water quality criteria for all rivers and streams of economic importance.
This is a big program but I do suggest it is not beyond the limits of a water control division, provided it has funds to undertake these studies. It would provide a great opportunity to graduates from our universities who are particularly interested in the conservation of renewable natural resources and, in this instance, all the problems related to the maintenance of a pure water supply for the Canadian people, and the improvement of situations where this does not exist at the present time.
I am very pleased with the work outlined by the Council of Resource Ministers. The council has a public relations officer, Mr. Walter Gray who is, I believe, ideally suited for this position because he is deeply interested in the conservation of natural resources of all types. He kindly came to give an address to the annual meeting of the Canadian Tree Fanners Association, of which I happen to be the president. He outlined the establishment of the council, how it operates, what it is intended to undertake, and so on. In the course of his speech he said:
The Council has so far held three plenary sessions. The first, as I have mentioned, was in Toronto in September, 1962. The second was in Montreal in November 1963, three months after the Secretariat was organized. At that time the Council authorized the Secretariat to carry out an inventory of the 70 Federal-Provincial and interprovincial resource agreements.
I think that was a good undertaking. Mr. Gray went on to say:
A review team was organized and worked until last September amassing data. The final draft of

712	COMMONS
Proposed Water Pollution Control the inventory is now being prepared for presentation to the Council at its next meeting, in Victoria, B.C., in May.
The Secretariat was given its second major assignment at the third plenary session in Prince Edward Island last June. At that time, Council agreed to sponsor a conference on water, air and soil pollution. The National conference, to be called, "Pollution and our Environment" will be held in Montreal in the Spring of 1966.
I see my time has almost expired, but I do wish to mention that there is a great deal of work to be done in this connection. I also wish to congratulate the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) on the excellent speech he made at the Northwest Pacific Trade Association held in Portland recently, in the course of which he emphasized the need for the conservation of our water resources in Canada and the determination of this Government to protect those resources for this and future generations before dealing with Government in the United States with respect to the export of water and so on. I was very glad to hear that.
The question of water conservation is a most important one and it has caught the imagination of many people. I noticed in today's Globe and Mail a report of a meeting addressed by Mr. Robert Turnbull, a Globe and Mail feature writer. He is another of the press men to whom I pay tribute. He is deeply interested in this question. Addressing the Sixth Convention of the Ontario Institute of Professional Agrologists and the Agricultural Institute of Canada he urged establishment of a Federal Department of Water Resources. He went on to say:
Geologists have warned that the demand for water in the United States may exceed the supply as early as 1970 These same geologists have added that the unpolluted river systems of Canada and Alaska could be tapped to meet U.S. demands.
Hence, a Federal agency is needed to protect Canada's most abundant resource. Hard on the heels of the Columbia River project-
I will not go into that now, because I could talk about it at some length-
-a proposal has been advanced to divert Canadian and Alaskan waters to the benefit of the West Coast states.
He went on to say:
The public is only casually aware of the growing crisis in water supply. Everywhere we turn nowadays we see people marching with signs damning The Bomb or segregation or a host of other ills, but have you ever seen any mass rising to shout about the water crisis?
Mr. Turnbull goes on to give examples of ancient civilizations which were destroyed as a result of the exhaustion of their water supplies. He points out that today the per capita
[Mr. Herridge.l

consumption of water in the United States is in excess of 560 gallons a day, and that this consumption is expected to double in the not distant future. Further on he writes:
Dangerous diseases have been transmitted by the pollution of U.S. tidal waters and the consumption of shellfish from these waters.
He ends by saying there is a possibility that the United States might annex Canada to gain access to our water resources. That is a bold prophecy. I hope it will never come about because of the attention paid by this Government and future Governments to this important question.

subtopic: SUGGESTED CREATION OF POLLUTION CONTROL DIVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Member who has introduced this motion is supposedly, according to the stories I have heard, going to retire. I have also heard him referred to as the Baron of the Kootenays, and I gather from the hon. Member's interest in this topic that he is determined that when he does retire and returns to his baronage, or whatever it is that a baron goes to, he shall have clean water there. I am not about to retire, I am not a baron, and I do not come from the Kootenays; but I agree with him wholeheartedly and commend him for bringing this topic forward because I do think it is a matter of interest and concern. During the Throne Speech debate I spoke about the problem of water pollution on the Great Lakes and I do not today want to rehash what I said then. I do think, though, that before I get into the specifics of the motion proposed by the hon. Member I should go back to a few of the fundamentals involved in this problem.
We all know that water is an essential resource. We all know that we have an ample supply of water for our present and forecast future needs in this country, provided we do not destroy the water that we have. There is ample evidence that we are destroying this water; we are in process of destroying this resource. This is why the problem has come before us now and is receiving attention generally throughout this country and the United States. The problem really varies in its severity and its nature from region to region across the country, but I think it is safe to say that virtually all waters that are surrounded by any large group of people are contaminated or polluted to some degree. It is also fair to say that the problem is probably most severe in the Great Lakes
April 28, 1985

region and possibly in the St. Lawrence region, particularly the Great Lakes because the water there does not flow swiftly. These are reservoirs, and the pollutants tend to collect and stay there. With faster moving streams, faster moving bodies of water, they tend to some degree to flush themselves. So the problem is probably most severe in the Great Lakes area.
I have some figures that I think are interesting and give some idea of the economic impact of this problem. They are figures that have been prepared by Dr. A. E. Berry, who was formerly, I believe, Chairman of the Ontario Water Resources Commission and is now Secretary-Treasurer of the Canadian Institute on Pollution Control. He has come up with some figures that give, Province by Province, an annual estimated cost of the pollution of our waters. I will give these figures now, Mr. Speaker: for the Province of British Columbia, $32 million per year; Alberta, $30 million; Saskatchewan, $20 million; Manitoba, $23 million; Ontario, $175 million; Quebec, $156 million; New Brunswick, $18 million; Nova Scotia, $18 million; Prince Edward Island, $2 million; Newfoundland, $10 million-for a total of $484 million per year. He has, in arriving at these figures, considered the cost of the following items. He has regarded the effects of pollution as affecting drinking water supplies, recreation in all forms, industry, agriculture, commercial fisheries, sport fishing, the effects of nutrients on the production of algae and other conditions in the waters, the build-up of chemical products, the destruction of fish and aquatic life by poisons, the effects of herbicides, pesticides, and so on. So he has come up with a figure of $484 million per year as the cost right now of the pollution of the water resources of this country. It is a significant amount of money; it is a significant problem, and let us see what really should be done to stop it.
On its face, it should be a simple problem to solve because there are only three real sources of pollution. First of all we have the pollution caused by the discharge of untreated or improperly treated sewage from our municipalities. The cure would appear simple. We just have to instal adequate sewage treatment plants in all our municipalities so that this pollution does not occur. In order to do this we require, really, two things. We require the necessary provincial legislation and we require a very, very large sum of money. I have no idea, because I have not been able to
Proposed Water Pollution Control get a reasonable figure, of how much money really would be required, but I do know that it would be substantial. A figure I gave in the Throne Speech debate indicated that Toronto, which has done a very good job of treating its sewage, would require another $300 million or so to do a completely adequate job. This is just one major community of many across this country.
The second source of pollution is industrial waste. Surely if industry would stop dumping pollutants into our streams, this would cure that problem. There has been an estimate-and I am quoting from an article in a Toronto paper, the Toronto Star of Thursday, April 22-that 30 per cent of industrial wastes in the Province of Ontario are discharged in a polluting condition into the waters, streams, rivers and lakes of that Province. The great need there is, (a) for legislation, and (b) money, so that industry can deal with this problem. I was very glad to see in the budget that was brought down on Monday that the Federal Government is going to allow tax concessions by allowing a depreciation rate of 50 per cent on capital works that are put in by industry so that industry will not dump raw pollutants into our waters. I had a notice of motion on the order paper that called for this sort of approach. I certainly do not claim any fatherhood for the item in the budget, but I am very glad to see that this step has been taken, because there is no use introducing legislation forcing industry to take this step if industry does not have the financial resources to do so. Therefore I think the item in the budget has gone a long way toward making it possible for the Provinces to enact legislation knowing that industry will be able to finance the capital works involved. It may be necessary, and I am not sure, to go even further and to allow industry that does not have sufficient capital to, possibly through the Industrial Development Bank, obtain a form of low interest loan to enable them to quickly put in the plant required. But that is the second part of the problem, industrial waste.
The third major source of pollution is from shipping, ships that discharge garbage and sewage as they ply the heavily travelled waterways of our country. To deal with this problem we need Federal legislation, amendments to the Shipping Act that will prevent ships from doing this and will prohibit them from doing it. We need, of course, the concurrence of our American friends, who share these waterways, that they will pass similar
714	COMMONS
Proposed Water Pollution Control legislation so that no ships, particularly those sailing through the St. Lawrence Seaway and the Great Lakes area will be allowed to discharge and dump sewage into these waters.
In addition to this we have the problem of pleasure craft in some of the smaller recreational areas in the country. I think of the Muskoka Lakes, that I am familiar with, in Northern Ontario where, because of the large numbers of pleasure craft plying those lakes, and lakes such as Lake Simcoe, there is a problem of pollution caused by their sewage. So I think the day is not very far away when we will have to pass legislation requiring pleasure craft to instal some form of container or tank so that raw sewage is not pumped from the boats into the water.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
If this is all we need do, these three things-stop municipalities from dumping sewage into the lakes, stop industry from doing that as well as preventing shipping from doing it-then why do we not go ahead and do this? What are the problems or difficulties which are holding us back? There are really four major deterrents or problems. First of all, there is the problem of co-ordination. Canada and the Great Lakes area and many of our streams and rivers are only half the problem; we must remember we share these bodies of water with another country.
Second, there is the cost required to deal with the problem. Vast sums of money are required by municipalities and by industries to put in the necessary treatment plants.
Third, there is the problem of public education so that various levels of government will be able to raise taxes and spend money for this purpose. Like the hon. Member for Kootenay West, I too commend those people in the press who have taken this problem to heart and are starting now to give it adequate publicity and treatment, so that the general public is informed.
The fourth thing which needs to be done concerns the problem of research. We do not have enough information about the methods of treatment. We do not have enough information about the tolerable levels of pollution which any stream or river can take. There is much more to be done in this area. In the Great Lakes work is being done by the United States. The Great Lakes Institute is also doing work on the Canadian side in this regard. But the amount of money the Great Lakes Institute has to work with is such that their funds from the Federal Government amount

DEBATES	April 26, 1965
to about $240,000 per annum, and that is all. When we consider that we are talking of losses in the Province of Ontario alone of around $175 million per year, it seems pretty paltry to spend $250,000 to do the fundamental and necessary research required for this problem.
I think we are starting now to take the correct steps toward a long term solution of the problem. The hon. Member for Kootenay West mentioned the conference which is going to be held in the spring of 1966 by the Council of Resource Ministers to deal with the specifics of air, water and land pollution. This meeting will be dealing with a whole series of topics and with the co-ordinating mechanisms between Federal and Provincial Governments which will be necessary so that concerted action can be taken to deal with the problem in the country.
Some of the topics they will be considering I think are worth putting on record. They are going to consider the historical perspective on environmental pollution and its control in Canada; the nature and sources of environmental contamination; the effects of such contamination on public health; the effects of such contamination on the national environment and economy; the pesticide contamination of the Canadian environment; the solid waste disposal and land improvements; radiation pollution; the extent of water pollution in the Provinces and the programs for its abatement; the participation of the Federal Government in investigations concerning pollution; programs of control-essentially legislation; industrial accomplishments in the control of pollution in Canada; criterion standards for a cleaner environment; the development of new instruments for measuring pollution; pollution control techniques; legal safeguards against pollution; an analysis on Canadian and other water pollution control organizations; and the economics of pollution control and methods for financing pollution control.
I think that if they study these topics carefully an adequate program and method can be devised to deal with the problem of pollution of our water, air and land resources. I think they will also be the only body in this country which can do that, because of the jurisdictional problem, where water resources are essentially a provincial resource. The Provinces have to enact legislation with respect thereto, yet the Federal Government has a certain part to play. Obviously it has a certain role to play in providing finance. This meeting which is planned for the spring of
April 28. 1965
1966 will, I think, be the answer to our pollution problems. I think it really meets the requirements of the motion suggested by the hon. Member, and for that reason I do not think we should pass the motion.
There are only two, I think, shortcomings in this program which the Resource Ministers will be putting forward. First, I am of the firm opinion that the Great Lakes region cannot wait for the long-term solution to the problem which this meeting will start to work on. I believe the Great Lakes requires action before the results of these meetings come forward. I believe the problem in the Great Lakes is simple enough-it only involves one Province-that we should now deal with that area.
Second, I think the Federal Government should now step up the sums of money it allocates to research in these fields. I do not think we require a Council of Resource Ministers to tell us we should be spending more than a quarter of a million dollars a year on research in this area, when the potential losses run in the region of half a billion dollars a year. To me this ratio does not look very reasonable, so I think we do not need a meeting of Resource Ministers to tell us of our shortcomings there.
Subject to action being taken quickly on the Great Lakes, and subject to action being taken to increase soon the amount of money we spend on research, I believe that the meetings scheduled for the spring of 1966 will meet the requirements of the motion proposed by the hon. Member for Kootenay West; and I believe they will meet the longterm needs of the country as far as dealing effectively with the problem of pollution of our water, and in addition our air and land, is concerned.

Mr. Speaker, the discussion which is taking place this afternoon is one of those discussions we have had over the years precipitated by the initiative of our good friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). It deals with a problem in which he has had a vital interest over a number of years. Indeed, during all the years I have been in this House I think the hon. Member for Kootenay West has provided an opportunity for Members to make a contribution to a consideration of the wise management and multiple use of our renewable resources, of which none is more vital than water.
As a result of these discussions which have taken place over the years, I do not think we
Proposed Water Pollution Control need any further background information as to the nature of the problem. It is true enough that for many years there was lethargy and indifference concerning the conservation of our water resources. But now, as a result of many recent activities, I feel that the attention of the nation has been aroused to the necessity for immediate and urgent action to come to grips with this one aspect of wise management of our water resources, namely the control of pollution.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that I, as one Member in this House, heartily support the motion which has been moved by the hon. Member for Kootenay West this afternoon. I think also that I can speak on behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, because certainly our activity during our brief term in office demonstrated in a clearcut way that we were not only interested in talking about this problem but also intended to proceed with immediate action.
