I thank the hon. Member for Kootenay West for those kind words.
There has already been some review made of the recent developments in this area of water control, so it is not necessary for me to recover that area of the subject.
The hon. Member for Broadview (Mr. Hahn) spoke a moment ago in reference to a conference to be sponsored by the Resource Ministers Council to be held in 1966, as the next great step forward in effective control of pollution. This development was contemplated by the Resource Ministers Council conference held in 1961. If there is any doubt about the adequacy of the background information on the subject and the delineation of the problem, Mr. Speaker, let me refer hon. Members to the voluminous reports which were made by that Resource Ministers Conference held in Montreal in 1961.
At that time this whole area of water control was thoroughly and exhaustively examined by the most competent people from all walks of life and areas of responsibility in Canada. One of the specific recommendations made by that conference related to the formation of a National Advisory Board on Water Conservation. That recommendation had the immediate support of the then Prime Minister and I would anticipate, and I do not think I am putting any thoughts into the mind of the mover of this resolution, that the sort of water pollution control division that he con-

April 28, 1965

Proposed Water Pollution Control templates would parallel very closely the functions of the National Advisory Board on Water Conservation, the establishment of which was the subject of one of the major recommendations of the Resources for Tomorrow Conference.
It is useful to note, Mr. Speaker, that the Government of Canada, and this House, and more recently the Resource Ministers Council and its supporting secretariat, have not waited for additional legislation before making a contribution to the solution of this problem. There are already existing Acts in force which can be used to come to immediate grips with the more extreme abuses. I refer, of course, to the fact that as soon as the Resource Ministers Council steering committee met to plan the conference it realized that the critical time was upon us, with the result that the Government in 1959 moved immediately to provide some means whereby municipalities could deal with local pollution problems. Sewage and water control legislation had been the means of direct action toward the control of pollution in most of the major municipalities across this nation.
Within the next few weeks my own City of Brandon will complete the construction and development of its first venture into the area of sewage control. This is a minor development, but it is typical of the kind of action municipalities have taken across Canada.
There is also in existence the Canada Water Conservation Act which was approved by Parliament in the early 1950's. This Act remained dormant until the latter 1950's, and up to the present time there have not been many major water control and conservation projects launched under the provisions of this Act.
Perhaps I should refer the hon. Member for Broadview to the major project which has been launched under the Canada Water and Conservation Act, namely the Metropolitan Toronto water conservation development which by now must be in its latter stages of development. This is being carried on under the direction of Dr. Berry, for the Province of Ontario, and the Division of Water and Resources of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. This is the first major co-operative attempt by the three levels of Government-Federal, Provincial and local-to come to grips with all aspects of water control and conservation in one of Canada's major metropolitan communities. The Federal contribution toward this project was some $14 million, and that will illustrate the vast sums of money which are required
[Mr. Dinsdale.)
to really provide a solution to this problem. That $14 million represented only 33J per cent of the total cost of that project.
To bring my brief remarks to a conclusion, in order that other hon. Members will have an opportunity to make a contribution to this discussion, let me suggest that we have observed various ad hoc, almost hit or miss, emergency projects. Up to this time sewage legislation has been of this ad hoc nature. The action contemplated by the Budget speech of Monday night, whereby industry will be able to derive some tax benefit from moves toward the control of industrial pollution is the kind of ad hoc, hit or miss project which has been developed in an attempt to correct this situation which has reached a critical state.
If the Resource Ministers Council can create the sort of organization that was recommended by the Resource Ministers Conference of 1961-at that time it was called the National Advisory Board on Water Conservation-I am sure that everything contemplated by the hon. Member in his resolution now before the House will be achieved.
I should also like to join with other Members who have spoken today in complimenting men such as Walter Gray who, at some personal sacrifice to his journalistic career, accepted the position of information officer for the newly formed Resource Ministers Council in order that he might devote his full attention to informing the public about the critical nature of this problem. Canada has been a land of limitless and renewable resources. The frontier concept of outward expansion has remained with us far too long. I think it is an encouraging sign that we have received agreement from all sides of this House today, and I hope that at long last the Governments of Canada at all levels will move together in a co-ordinated way to ensure that this most vital of all our renewable resources will be preserved and conserved for the future.

subtopic: SUGGESTED CREATION OF POLLUTION CONTROL DIVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words as a private Member from what is probably one of the most water resource rich constituencies in Canada, that of Coast-Capilano. We have a long seacoast and a number of substantial rivers and streams, and the people of that area are very much concerned, of course, with pollution as well as other matters of water management. I should like to make several suggestions in the few minutes left to me and they are made in my private capacity.
First, I should like to see the very excellent provision contained in the budget with regard to a fast two year write-off on machinery and equipment structures for water pollution control, extended to air pollution control. I think this would be very desirable and would result in measures generally beneficial to the rest of our society, particularly society other than industry. I should like to see special grants made available for research into pollution control not only in respect of water pollution but also air pollution. I should like to see one department of Government in Ottawa assigned the responsibility for looking after the management of water matters, including not just power and navigation but also pollution control, etc. In other words, the multipurpose use of water should be looked at comprehensively by one department to which this responsibility has been specifically assigned.
I should like to see more effective machinery set up for Federal-Provincial and even
Proposed Water Pollution Control Federal-Provincial-Municipal co-operation in respect of water matters. In this country the jurisdiction with regard to pollution is divided between the Federal authority and the Provincial authority in a fashion which does not lead toward an administratively easy approach, at least, to a matter which should be attacked on all fronts simultaneously. In summarizing that position I should like to quote Professor Bora Laskin who was one of the contributors to the Resources for Tomorrow Conference which has been referred to by other Members who have spoken today. Under the heading "Jurisdictional Framework For Water Management" there is the following in a summary of a paper he gave in 1961:
Legislative regulation, or even extinction, of these private and public rights and legislative control of other aspects of water resources are, in some respects, within federal and, in others, within provincial competence. Federal authority is comprehensive with respect to land and water lots owned by the Federal Crown. Where, however, it must rely on legislative power only, it is doubtful that its navigation power is ample enough to justify ancillary regulation of water power rights, flood protection, pollution and the like. Yet provincial legislative power in these matters, otherwise fairly broad, is subject to the paramount authority of Parliament in relation to navigation and shipping, and fisheries. Limited power exists in Parliament under its criminal law power, e.g. as to prohibition of pollution, but short of conceding to its authority to legislate in the interest of general public health, regulation here rests in general with the Provinces.
There are some gaps other than this very difficult constitutional one which I think can be plugged either by the Federal Government acting on its own initiative or by the Provinces acting unilaterally on their own initiative. One is in respect of the pollution of waters immediately offshore. We had an expensive but interesting example of this in my own riding last year. A barge roughly 150 feet long and carrying 9,000 barrels of oil sank a few miles offshore from West Vancouver. This hulk sank in roughly 300 feet of water It was worth some $25,000. It was estimated initially that rescue operations would run to several times that amount, so the barge was abandoned. The hulk was no longer of value to the private oil company concerned and it was left for the rest of our community either to leave it there, in which case it would constitute a hazard over the long term because it would ultimately tear open, and also in the short term because it was leaking, or to get the Federal Government to do something. The Federal Government had to move in this connection, and it
718	COMMONS
Proposed Water Pollution Control did so to the extent of some four months of effort and an eventual cost of more than a quarter of a million dollars.
The barge was raised and its contents were sold for a fraction of the cost of raising it. The result was that the Federal treasury, in the last analysis Canadian taxpayers, was left to foot the bill. There is a large gap in our Federal legislation in this respect. It should be possible for the Federal Government to move against someone for negligence of this type. This vessel was afloat, admittedly in a sinking condition, for several hours before it sank. Something could have been done about it had action been taken early enough, and possibly action could have been taken by the private interests. At the very least there
DEBATES	April 28, 1965
should be legislation to take care of cases of this kind.
